column2: Delighting in the acquisition of treasure, like Vaishravana (Kubera), knowing the ten classes, one whose nature is to attend to rise and decline of stations;
a king should be the supporter of the unsupported and the overseer of the supported, of pleasant face and speaking first with a smile.
Attending the elders, having conquered sloth, free of greed, with his mind set on the conduct of the good, for the good see conduct.
He should never take wealth from the hands of the good, but take it from the wicked and give it to the good.
Himself a striker and a giver, with self subdued and means subdued, giving and enjoying at the proper time, and of pure conduct.

He should make helpers of the brave, devoted, those who cannot be seduced, those born in good families, the healthy, the well-behaved and those connected with the well-behaved, the self-respecting who do not slight others,
those versed in learning, knowers of the world, those who look to the next world, devoted to dharma, the good, unshaken as mountains.
A king honouring prosperity should always make such his helpers, and be equal to them in enjoyments, differing only by the umbrella and greater knowledge.
His conduct should always be visible and invisible; so doing, a king here finds no distress.
A king who suspects everyone and who takes everything is soon crooked and greedy, and is overthrown by his own people.
A pure king devoted to winning the mind of the world is not overthrown by enemies, and even fallen, stands.
Free of anger, without vices, mild in punishment, with senses subdued, a king becomes trustworthy to beings like the Himalaya.
Wise, endowed with the qualities of justice, intent on others' weak points, of good sight, knowing the policy and impolicy of all classes,
quick in action, anger conquered, graciously disposed, great-minded, healthy by nature, active, not boastful—
the king in whose realm undertakings are seen begun but not left unfinished is the best of kings.
The king in whose domain people go about fearless as sons in their father's house is the best of kings.
The king whose townsfolk and country folk have unconcealed wealth and know policy and impolicy is the best of kings.
The king whose people living in the realm are intent on their own work, not fond of combination, self-controlled, protected duly,
obedient, guidable, trained, not quarrelsome, and in whose domain men delight in giving—he is a true king.
In whose domain there is no deceit, fraud, illusion or envy, for that lord of the earth dharma is eternal.
He who honours the learned, who is guidable, devoted to the welfare of the townspeople, follows the dharma of the good and is a giver, is fit for kingship.
He whose spy and counsel and what is done and undone are never known to enemies is fit for kingship.
And this verse was sung of old by the great-souled Bhargava (Ushanas) in recounting Rama's story to a king, Bharata:
One should find a king first, then a wife, then wealth; if there is no king in the world, whence wife, whence wealth?
Therefore, king, for lions among kings there is no other eternal dharma than clear protection; protection upholds the world.
Two verses were recited by Manu son of Prachetas on the duties of kings, king of kings; hear them with a single mind.
A man should abandon these six, like a broken boat on the sea: a teacher who does not teach, a priest who has not studied,
a king who does not protect, a wife who speaks unpleasantly, a cowherd who longs for a village, and a barber who longs for a forest.
The revered Vishalaksha, the great ascetic Kavya (Shukra), the thousand-eyed Mahendra, and Manu son of Prachetas,
the revered Bharadvaja, and the sage Gaurashiras, authors of the science of kings, devoted to Brahmanas and expounders of Brahma,
all praise protection alone as the dharma, best of upholders of dharma, lotus-eyed; and hear the means of kings in this.
Spies and the stationing of agents, giving at the proper time without envy, taking by proper method and not taking by improper method, Yudhishthira,
gathering the good, valour, skill, truth, welfare of the subjects, splitting the enemy's side by uprightness and crookedness,
not abandoning the good, sustaining those of good family, accumulating what is to be accumulated, serving the wise,
ever cheering the troops, attending to the subjects, untiring in affairs, and increasing the treasury,
guarding the city, not trusting, dividing the city's combinations, and attending to old houses and those in distress.
Brihaspati declared exertion the root of kings' dharma; hear from me the verses on this:
By exertion the nectar was won; by exertion the asuras were slain; by exertion Mahendra gained pre-eminence here and in heaven.
A man steady in exertion overcomes those steady in speech; those steady in speech wait on one steady in exertion.
A king lacking exertion, even though wise, is always open to attack by enemies, as a venomless snake is.
An enemy is not to be scorned, even if weak, by the strong; fire, though small, burns, and a little poison kills.
An enemy raised even with a single horse, resting on a fort, torments this or that country even of a prosperous king.
What is the king's secret word, for victory and for the gathering of the world, what is crooked in his heart and what is for a reason,
and what is his deed of fault, is held with uprightness alone; for deceiving the world he should practise a most righteous conduct.
Kingship is a very great system, hard to bear for the unrefined; it cannot be borne by a gentle man, a supreme station of blows.
Kingship is always a flesh-meal (all prey), borne here by uprightness; therefore one should always act with a mixture, Yudhishthira.
Even if misfortune comes to him while protecting, that too is his great dharma; for kings are so conducted.
This is a portion of the duties of kings described to you; ask me where you have further doubt, best of speakers."
Then the revered Vyasa, Devasthana with Ashma, Vasudeva, Kripa, Satyaki and Sanjaya,
delighted, with faces as if swelling, said "Well done, well done," and praised Bhishma, tiger among men, best of upholders of dharma.
Then the best of the Kurus, dejected, with eyes full of tears, softly touching his feet, said to Bhishma:
Tomorrow I shall ask about my doubts, grandsire; the sun too is setting, having drunk the earth's savour.
Then Keshava, Kripa, and those Yudhishthira and others, circumambulating the son of the great river, joyfully mounted their chariots.
And bathing in the Drishadvati, of good vows, having performed the water-rite and recited auspicious prayers, scorchers of foes, duly performing the twilight, they entered the city of Gajahvaya.
Reaching Kurukshetra and approaching the blameless Bhishma, asking the best of chariot-warriors, Gangeya, of the night's comfort,
saluting Vyasa and the other sages and welcomed by them all, they sat around Bhishma, surrounding him.
Then King Yudhishthira, greatly radiant, king of dharma, with joined palms, having honoured and saluted Bhishma, said:

This word 'king, king' that is current, Bharata—how did this arise? Tell me that, grandsire.
mahabharata:12:59.6	With equal hands, head and neck, of equal intellect, senses and self, of equal joy and sorrow, equal back, arms and belly,
mahabharata:12:59.7	of equal semen, bone and marrow, equal flesh and blood, equal inhaling and exhaling, with equal life and body,
mahabharata:12:59.8	equal in birth and death, equal in all qualities of men—how does one rule over the more intelligent and the brave?
mahabharata:12:59.9	How does one guard the whole earth, thronged with heroes, brave men and nobles, and how does the world desire his favour?
mahabharata:12:59.11	I wish to hear all this truly, bull of the Bharatas; tell me as it is, best of speakers.
mahabharata:12:59.12	This cause cannot be slight, lord of men, that the whole world submits to one, god-like.
[Bhishma said:] "Be attentive, best of men; hear everything entirely, how kingship arose in the beginning, in the Krita age.
There was neither kingdom nor king, nor rod nor wielder of it; all subjects protected one another by dharma alone.
Protecting one another by dharma, Bharata, men came to supreme distress, and then delusion entered them.
Fallen under the sway of delusion, those men, bull among men, through bewilderment of understanding lost their dharma.
When understanding was lost, men under delusion, then all fell under the power of greed, best of the Bharatas.
Then, laying hands on what they had not obtained, another thing arose among them, lord, named desire.
Those fallen under desire were touched by passion, and, reddened, did not know what should and should not be done, Yudhishthira.
They did not give up forbidden intercourse, what should and should not be said, what is edible and not, or what is fault and non-fault.
When this world of men was in confusion, Brahma was lost; and by the loss of Brahma, O king, dharma came to destruction.
When Brahma and dharma were lost, the gods fell into fear; frightened, tiger among men, they went to Brahma for refuge.
Reaching the revered grandsire of the world, all the gods, with joined palms, afflicted with sorrow, grief and fear, said:
'Revered one, the eternal Brahma that dwelt in the world of men is lost; by states such as greed and delusion fear has entered us.
By the loss of Brahma, lord, dharma too has perished; then we have become equal with mortals, lord of the three worlds.
Our rain falls below, and mortals send rain upward; from the cessation of their rites we have come to doubt.
Meditate, grandsire, on what is the best for us here; from your power that power of ours does not perish.'
Then the self-existent revered one said to all those gods: 'I shall think of what is good; let your fear go, best of gods.'
Then he composed, born of his own intellect, a work of a hundred thousand chapters, in which dharma, wealth and desire were described.
This group was famed as the triple aim by the Self-existent himself; the fourth, liberation, is a separate aim and a separate group.
Another triad of liberation is declared: sattva, rajas and tamas; and the station, growth and decline; and the triad born of the rod.
Self, place and time, means, task, helpers and cause: the sixfold group is held to be born of policy.
The triple learning, logic and trade, Bharata, and the great science of the rod-policy were set forth as learnings there.
Protection of ministers, the stationing of agents, protection of the prince, spies and various expedients, and different kinds of stationed agents;
conciliation, gifts, division and the rod, Pandava, and indifference as the fifth were set out entirely.
Counsel is fully described, and its purpose of division, the leakage of counsel and the fruit of its success and failure.
Treaty of various names, low, middle and highest, called by fear, honour and wealth, is fully described.
The four times of marching, the expansion of the triple aim, victory joined to dharma, victory by wealth,
and victory by the asura method are fully described; the marks of the fivefold group are described in three kinds.
The rod is called open and secret; the open is eightfold, the secret has many details.
Chariots, elephants, horses and foot-soldiers, Pandava, forced labour, boats, spies and guides on the road, as eight;
these are the open limbs of the army, Kaurava; moving and unmoving, powders and compounds such as poisons are mentioned.
In touch and in food, secret ways of many kinds are remembered; enemy, friend and neutral are also described.
All the merits of roads and of land, self-protection, reassurance, and the watching of spies,
various arrays of men, elephants, chariots and horses, formations of various names, wondrous skill in fighting,
sallies and falls, good fighting and good retreat, knowledge of the use of weapons, bull of the Bharatas,
the army's misfortune and its cheering, times of oppression and assault, times of fear, Pandava,
and the construction of ditches, the movement of yoga, the oppression of an enemy kingdom by robbers, forest tribes and the weak and fierce,
by fire-setters and poisoners, by false agents, by negotiation with chiefs of guilds, by cutting down creepers,
by defiling elephants, by raising suspicion, by blockade, by cutting off food and roads,
the decline and growth of the realm of seven parts, the capacity of envoys, the use of yoga and the increase of the kingdom,
the deception of friends situated among the enemy, rightly stated; crushing and counterstrike against the stronger,
very subtle administration, weeding out thorns, peace, exertion and yoga, and gathering of wealth,
supporting the unsupported and watching the supported, giving at the proper time for aims, and not indulging in vices,
and the king's qualities and the qualities of the general, and the merits and faults of cause and doer,
signs of the wicked of many kinds, the behaviour of dependants, suspicion of everyone, and the avoiding of carelessness,
desire to obtain what is not obtained, increase of what is obtained, and giving duly to worthy recipients what has increased,
spending of wealth for dharma, for wealth, for desire, and fourth, when blows of misfortune come, are likewise described here.
Ten vices, born of anger and of desire, fierce, are mentioned here, best of the Kurus.
Hunting, dice, drink and women, bull of the Bharatas, are called by the teachers the vices born of desire, said here by the Self-existent himself.
Harshness of speech, fierceness, harshness of punishment, self-restraint, giving up and ruin of wealth are those born of anger.
Various machines and their operations are described, crushing, counterstrike, the breaking of banners,
trampling shrine-trees, blockade, destruction of works, plunder, going and halting are described.
Of drums, tabors, conches and kettledrums, best of warriors, and the acquisition of wealth, and the six kinds of crushing.
Pacification of what is obtained, honouring the good, union with the learned, knowing the morning oblation rite,
auspicious touching, remedy of the body, regulation of food, and constant faith,
rising by oneself, truthfulness, sweet speech, and rites at festivals and assemblies, and banner-born (state) rites,
conduct in all offices, visible and invisible, bull of the Bharatas, and constant supervision,
exemption of Brahmanas from punishment, applying the rod with discretion, protection by dependants from their own castes in their merits,
protection of the townsfolk, increase of one's own kingdom, and the thought on the circle of states, the twelve kings, O king,
and the seventy-two said by the Self-existent, the dharmas of countries, castes and families, are fully described.
Dharma, wealth, desire and liberation are described here, and means and desire for wealth with various large fees.
Root-work and action and the use of illusion are described here, and the defiling of streams and of still waters is described.
By whatever means the world would not stray from the noble path—all that, tiger among kings, is described in the science of policy.
Having made this auspicious work, the revered lord, glad, then said to all the gods led by Shakra:
'For the benefit of the world and the establishment of the triple aim, this fresh butter of Sarasvati, this wisdom, has been produced.
Joined to the rod, it protects the world, delighting in restraint and favour; it will go about the worlds.
The world is led by the rod, and the rod leads; thus it is called the policy of the rod and pervades the three worlds.
This essence of the merits of the sixfold policy will stand ahead among the great-souled; because of the greatness of the rod, the policy has clear marks.
Policy and conduct are vast, by which all this is pervaded; and the tradition of the Puranas and the births of great sages,
the lines of tirthas and families, of stars, Yudhishthira, the whole fourfold stage of life, and likewise the four hotri priests,
the four classes and the four Vedas are described here, and the Itihasa, the Upavedas and all logic are described.
Austerity, knowledge, non-violence, truth and untruth, supreme policy, serving the elders, giving, purity and exertion,
compassion for all beings—everything is described here; whatever is the range of speech on earth is all included.
In that science of the Grandsire, Pandava, without doubt dharma, wealth, desire and liberation are all declared.'
Then the revered Shankara first took up that policy: the many-formed, broad-eyed Shiva Sthanu, lord of Uma.
Knowing the decline of ages and of life, the revered Shiva then condensed the work of great meaning made by Brahma.
It was called the Vaishalaksha, and Indra received it; the great ascetic Subrahmanya condensed it into ten thousand chapters.
The revered Purandara too condensed that work, dear one, into five thousand, which is called the Bahudantaka.
Brihaspati, the lord, condensed it by his intellect into three thousand chapters; it is called the Barhaspatya.
Kavya (Ushanas) condensed it into a thousand chapters, that teacher of yoga of immeasurable wisdom and great austerity.
Thus, in accordance with the world, this work was condensed by the great sages, knowing the diminution of the life of mortals, Pandava.
Then the gods assembled and said to Vishnu the Prajapati: 'Appoint the one who deserves pre-eminence among mortals.'
Then, reflecting, the revered god Narayana, the lord, created from his mind a son of splendour, free of rajas.
But that Viraja, greatly fortunate, did not desire lordship on earth; his wisdom was devoted to renunciation, Pandava.
His son was Kirtiman, who also went beyond the five; his son was Kardama, who also practised great austerity.
Kardama the Prajapati's son was named Ananga, a protector of subjects, good, skilled in the policy of the rod.
Ananga's son, Atibala, learned in policy, obtained the kingdom of the earth, and then came under the sway of the senses.
The daughter of Death, mind-born, named Sunitha, famed in the three worlds, bore Vena.
Him, who did unrighteous things among the subjects, following passion and hatred, the sages, expounders of Brahma, struck down with kusha grass purified by mantras.
The sages then churned his right thigh with mantras, and from it was born a deformed, short-limbed man on earth.
Like a burnt stump, red-eyed and black-haired, the expounders of Brahma said to him, "Sit down."
From him came the Nishadas, cruel dwellers in hills and forests, and the other barbarians dwelling in the Vindhya by the hundred thousand.
Again those great sages churned his right hand, and a man arose, in form like another Indra.
Armoured, with sword bound, with arrows and bow, versed in the Vedas and their limbs and master of archery,
to that best of men the whole rod-policy attached itself, O king; then Vena's son with joined palms said to those great sages:
'A very subtle understanding has arisen in me, seeing dharma and wealth; what is to be done by me with it? Tell me truly.
Whatever work joined to wealth you tell me, I shall do; there is no need for doubt here.'
Then the gods and the great sages said to him: 'Without fear practise where dharma is fixed.
Casting off the liked and disliked, equal to all beings, casting far off desire, anger, greed and pride,
any man in the world who departs from dharma, you should restrain with your arms, ever looking to dharma.
And ascend the pledge by mind, deed and word: "I shall protect earthly Brahma," saying this repeatedly.
And what is declared here in the policy of dharma and rests on the rod-policy, I shall practise without fear, never by my own will.
And promise, lord: "Brahmanas shall be exempt from punishment by me, and I shall save the world from mixture of classes," scorcher of foes.'
Vena's son then said to those gods led by the sages: 'If Brahmanas are my helpers, so be it, best of gods.'
So be it, said Vena's son, told by those expounders of Brahma, and Shukra, a treasure made of Brahma, became his priest.
The Valakhilyas were his ministers, the Sarasvata group, and the revered great sage Garga became his astrologer.
Eight with himself—this is the supreme scripture among men. Two bards, charioteer and Magadha, were born for him earlier."
[Gautami said:] "If you two, Death and the serpent, are both under Time's sway, how could there be delight and anger? I wish to know this."
[Vyasa said:] "In the Krita age, long ago, Manu was the lord who bore the rod; his son, the great archer, was famed as Prajati.
King Yudhishthira son of Kunti did not know of it, nor the white-horsed one (Arjuna), nor Kunti, nor the renowned Draupadi.
The food prepared for Brahmanas for those great souls they gave, scented, to the monkeys.
He scorned bow-wielders, and all of Phalguna; as was said, so it should be done by one who wishes prosperity.
Hearing the words of those speaking piteously, the compassionate one said, "Alas, what hardship!" and Yudhishthira stood still.
